newsitem.title: FRANCE: Shell France says no plan to axe Berre refinery.
newsitem.headline: Shell France says no plan to axe Berre refinery.

text.p: Royal Dutch/Shell's French subsidiary has no plans to mothball its 128,000 barrel per day refinery at Berre in southeastern France, a spokesman said on Tuesday.
The Anglo/Dutch oil group said in a statement earlier it supported a French study's findings that southeastern France faced a surplus of oil refinery capacity.
Shell said it was "actively evaluating options, including participation in an industry rationalisation."
London analysts said the statement, appended to an annnouncement on a partial shake-up of Shell's European refinery and lubricant operations, might be a step towards closing Berre.
A Shell France spokesman said the plant would be kept open.
"No," he said, asked by Reuters whether Shell had any plans to close the plant.
"This refinery is next to a petrochemical complex which Shell has identified as an important one for the Mediterranean area. So we need the refinery to feed the petrochemicals plant."
He said however that talks had started with other refinery operators near Berre on a possible shared reduction in capacity to erase a glut of spare refining capacity for making gasoline.
He did not name the other companies involved.
Berre is one of four refineries clustered around the port of Marseilles. The other three are operated by Esso France, Total and BP France.

BP's Lavera refinery in the area is currently up for sale. The Shell spokesman suggested any coordinated plan to reduce capacity and boost profitability might make BP think again if it were put together in time for BP's early-1997 sale deadline.
"If something is there, then why not?," he said.
BP was not immediately available for comment.
Any plans to alter oil refining investments need government approval under French oil legislation, the Shell spokesman said.
A memorandum of understanding on possible rationalisation is being prepared for the industry ministry by the end of January.

Shell announced the possibility of joint industry action to cut capacity as striking oil workers virtually shut down the Berre complex and disruption production down at the three neighbouring local plants in a one-day dispute over job cuts.
A spokesman for France's largest union slammed the timing of Shell's announcement, saying it could harden the strike.
"You don't discuss this type of thing when the climate is already hot," the official from Socialist union CFDT said.
Shell France denied there was any deliberate link, saying a Swiss refinery sale that was also announced on Tuesday had to be disclosed to employees before internal meetings later this week.
"It was a pure coincidence," the spokesman said.
In London, Paul Skinner, a director of Shell International Petroleum, said Shell hoped to announce a definitive policy towards Berre, which employs 400 people, in January.
